courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: A transformer transfers energy between two circuits by mutual induction: a primary winding of N1 turns and a secondary of N2 turns on a laminated soft-iron core, the core increasing the magnetic flux and carrying it from one coil to the other. It works only on AC, because the secondary emf is -N2 dPhi/dt and a steady DC current gives a steady core flux and hence zero induced emf.

The transformer equation V2/V1 = N2/N1 (voltages rms, in volts; turns are pure numbers) follows because the same changing core flux threads every turn of both windings, so V1 = -N1 dPhi/dt and V2 = -N2 dPhi/dt give V1/N1 = V2/N2. N2 > N1 is step-up, N2 < N1 is step-down, N2 = N1 is an isolation transformer; the frequency of the output always equals that of the source.

In an ideal transformer there are no winding or core losses, so P1 = P2, i.e. V1 I1 = V2 I2 and I1/I2 = N2/N1 = V2/V1: the current ratio is the inverse of the voltage ratio, so voltage is gained only at the cost of current and no energy is created. Real efficiency is eta = P_out/P_in x 100%, typically 90-99%.

A transformer also transforms resistance: a load R on the secondary appears to the source as R_apparent = (N1/N2)^2 R, with the SQUARE of the turns ratio. Choosing the turns ratio so that this equals the source's own internal resistance is impedance matching, which gives maximum power transfer from source to load.

Real losses and their cures: copper loss (I^2 R heating in the windings, reduced by thicker low-resistance conductors, and load-dependent); eddy-current loss (currents induced in the core, reduced by laminating it into thin insulated sheets); hysteresis loss (energy per cycle to reverse the core's magnetisation, reduced by a soft magnetic material); plus flux leakage and mechanical/humming loss. Eddy and hysteresis are core losses and continue at no load.

Power is transmitted at high voltage because for a fixed delivered power P the line current is I = P/V, so the line waste is P_loss = I^2 R_line = P^2 R_line / V^2 and falls as the inverse square of the transmission voltage; AC beats DC for distribution precisely because transformers can step the voltage up for the line and back down for homes and businesses.

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: Net change / accumulation: if a quantity changes at rate r(t) then the total change over [a,b] is ∫ₐᵇ r(t) dt = f(b) − f(a); the units of the integral are (units of r)×(units of t), which is what identifies the answer as litres, joules, newtons, naira or kilograms. The average value of the rate is (1/(b−a))∫ₐᵇ r dt, not r at the midpoint.

Kinematics: antidifferentiate a(t) to get v(t) and v(t) to get s(t), each step fixed by an initial condition (v(0), s(0)). Displacement over [a,b] is ∫ₐᵇ v dt; total distance is ∫ₐᵇ |v| dt, obtained by splitting the interval at the zeros of v and adding magnitudes.

Work by a variable force: W = ∫ₐᵇ F(x) dx, valid because the force is effectively constant on a slice of width dx. For a spring obeying Hooke's law F = kx (k from a measured force and extension), W = ½k(b² − a²); F × d is only correct for a constant force.

Fluid force on a vertically submerged plate: pressure at depth h is ρgh, so the strip at depth h of width w(h) carries force ρg·h·w(h)dh and F = ρg∫ₐᵇ h·w(h) dh, with h measured downwards from the free surface (water: ρg = 9800 N/m³). Equivalent check: F = ρg·h̄·A with h̄ the centroid depth.

Marginal analysis: C(q) = ∫₀^q MC dq + C(0) where C(0) is fixed cost, and the extra cost from q₁ to q₂ is ∫(q₁)^(q₂) MC dq with no fixed cost involved; likewise R(q) = ∫₀^q MR dq. Profit change is ∫(MR − MC) dq and is maximised where MR = MC, an output the fixed cost cannot move.

Consumer and producer surplus: solve D(q) = S(q) for the equilibrium (q₀, p₀), then CS = ∫₀^(q₀)[D(q) − p₀]dq (area between the demand curve and the price line) and PS = ∫₀^(q₀)[p₀ − S(q)]dq (area between the price line and the supply curve); their sum is the total surplus used to judge market efficiency.

Environmental science: the cumulative amount of pollutant discharged over [0,T] is ∫₀^T r(t) dt, with ∫₀^T Ae^(kt) dt = (A/k)(e^(kT) − 1); population change is P(T) = P₀ + ∫₀^T r(t) dt, and constant relative growth P′ = kP gives P = P₀e^(kt).

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: The software testing life cycle: six phases in sequential order — requirement analysis, test planning, test case development, test environment setup, test execution, test cycle closure — each with an entry point where it begins and an exit point reached only when all the objectives of that phase have been achieved.

What each STLC phase owns: requirement analysis decides what is to be tested (document review, stakeholder interviews, issue identification); test planning fixes strategy, cost, duration and roles; test case development writes and reviews cases specifying inputs, process and expected outputs; test environment setup specifies software and hardware; test execution runs, retests and reports; test cycle closure confirms objectives met, writes the summary report and collects feedback.

Debugging as the process of identifying and resolving errors or bugs in a software system, distinct from testing, which only finds out whether the given output matches the expected output. Its methods are code inspection, monitoring, logging, unit, integration and system testing, and debugging tools — debuggers (Radare2, WinDbg, Valgrind), trace tools and profilers.

Functional testing methods, which check that the program performs as expected: unit testing on execution paths within functions, integration testing of how parts work together (top-down tests higher-level modules first, bottom-up tests lower-level modules first), system testing of the integrated whole against technical and functional requirements, and acceptance testing against expected requirements.

Non-functional testing methods, which check how well the software behaves rather than what it does: usability testing by observing users, performance testing for network, database and client-side delays under different load conditions, security testing for data security, availability, confidentiality and integrity, and compatibility testing across browsers, platforms and operating systems.

Black box, white box and grey box testing, separated purely by how much of the internal structure the tester knows: black box (unknown; integration, system, acceptance), white box (known, inputs chosen to exercise paths through the code, programming know-how essential; unit, integration, system), grey box (partially known, internals used to design the cases but tests run at the user level; primarily integration).

Designing test data in practice: equivalence partitioning takes one representative from each class the program should treat identically, boundary value analysis adds the values just below, at and just above each edge, and a debugger's breakpoint, step and variable watch locate where program state first becomes wrong so the defect class can be named.

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Stress σ = F/A in N/m² (Pa), strain ε = Δℓ/ℓ (dimensionless), and Hooke's law σ = Eε, valid only below the proportional limit.
Young modulus E = stress/strain = Fℓ/(AΔℓ), unit N/m² = Pa; a measure of stiffness, about 70 GPa for aluminium and 120 GPa for copper. (The deck misprints the unit as N/m.)
Central depression of a beam of length ℓ loaded with mass m at its midpoint: Y = mgℓ³/(48EI), the beam treated as two opposite cantilevers, g = 9.8 m/s².
Rectangular cross-section second moment I = bd³/12 (b = breadth, d = thickness), giving the linear working equation Y = mgℓ³/(4Ebd³).
Graph of depression Y (m) against load m (kg): a straight line through the origin of gradient s = gℓ³/(4Ebd³) in m/kg, hence E = gℓ³/(4bd³s).

Apparatus (dial gauge, beams of different materials, set of masses, 2 mounts), the 50 g to 500 g loading procedure, and the dominant error: d is cubed, so a 5% error in thickness gives about 15% error in E.

checks.topic: Conceptual session on Week 12 applications of integration exactly as the deck builds them: integrating a rate over an interval to get an accumulated total; why an initial condition is needed for an indefinite integral and why the constant cancels in a definite one; the fluid-force formula F = ∫ₐᵇ w·h(x)·L(x)dx with w = ρg; why a varying force forces W = ∫ₐᵇ F(x)dx instead of force × distance; recovering TR from MR and K from I(t); why equilibrium must be found before CS = ∫₀^Q₀[D(Q) − P₀]dQ and PS = ∫₀^Q₀[P₀ − S(Q)]dQ; and the cumulative-consumption model C(t) = 1000e^(0.035t) − 1000.

questions.q: In her first kinematics example the car's velocity is v(t) = 2t² + 6t + 1 kmh⁻¹ and she computes ∫₀⁵ v(t)dt. What kind of quantity does that integral produce, and why?
options: A distance in km, because integrating a rate of change of position over an interval accumulates the total change over that interval
A speed in kmh⁻¹, because the integral of a velocity is still a velocity
An acceleration, because integration and differentiation both change the physical quantity by one step
A distance, but only because the interval happens to start at t = 0
questions.concept: Integrating a rate over an interval gives the accumulated total
questions.why: Velocity is the rate of change of position, so ∫ₐᵇ v dt is the accumulated change in position between a and b — the units multiply out as (km/h)(h) = km. Option 2 confuses the integrand with the integral; v(5) = 81 km/h is the speed at the end, and it is the most common wrong answer in this whole week. Option 3 has the direction of the operation backwards: differentiating position gives velocity, so integrating velocity returns to position, never to acceleration. Option 4 is a misreading — the accumulation argument works for any limits a and b; starting at 0 only makes the lower bracket vanish arithmetically.

questions.q: In Example 2 she writes x(t) = ∫(6t² − 6t − 12)dt = 2t³ − 3t² − 12t + C and only then uses the words 'initial displacement is −4 m'. Why does she need that sentence at all?
options: Because the velocity function alone is not enough to integrate
Because the indefinite integral gives a whole family of displacement functions, and the datum picks the one member of the family that describes this body
Because the constant of integration is otherwise assumed to be zero by convention
Because displacement must always be measured from a negative starting point
questions.concept: What an initial condition does to an indefinite integral
questions.why: Every function 2t³ − 3t² − 12t + C has the same derivative, so the velocity alone cannot distinguish them; they differ only in where the origin sits. The datum x(0) = −4 selects C = −4 and so selects one curve. Option 1 is false — the integration is done before the datum is used. Option 3 states a convention where there is none: assuming C = 0 would put the body at the origin at t = 0, contradicting the question. Option 4 mistakes an arbitrary feature of this example for a rule.

questions.q: Part (c) of Example 2 asks for the net displacement in the first 5 seconds, and the −4 does not appear anywhere in her working. What is the reason?
options: She dropped it by mistake; it should have been carried through
Net displacement is always measured from the origin, so any starting offset is ignored by definition
A definite integral is F(5) − F(0), so any constant added to F appears in both terms and cancels
The constant only matters for velocity functions, not for displacement functions
questions.concept: Why the constant of integration cancels in a definite integral
questions.why: With antiderivative F(t) + C, the theorem gives (F(5) + C) − (F(0) + C) = F(5) − F(0); the C cancels, which is why the bracket on her slide reads [2t³ − 3t² − 12t]₀⁵. Option 1 is wrong and worth being sure about — carrying the −4 in and subtracting once gives 111, which is the position x(5), not the change. Option 2 has it exactly backwards: net displacement ignores the offset because it is a change, not because it is measured from the origin. Option 4 invents a distinction the mathematics does not make.

questions.q: Why does the dam problem need an integral rather than a single multiplication of pressure by area?
options: Because the dam face is not flat
Because the weight density of water is not constant over 100 m of depth
Because the width L(x) of the dam changes with depth
Because the pressure grows with depth, so no one pressure acts on the whole face; each thin strip is at essentially one depth and the integral adds the strips
questions.concept: Why fluid force on a vertical face is an integral
questions.why: Pressure at depth h is w·h, so it runs from 0 at the surface to a maximum at the base; multiplying any single pressure by the whole area is therefore wrong, and slicing into horizontal strips of near-constant depth is what makes the multiplication legitimate on each piece. Option 1 is false — this dam face is a flat rectangle. Option 2 is false: w = ρg = 9800 is a constant and she pulls it straight out of the integral. Option 3 is false for this example specifically — L(x) = 300 everywhere, which is why 9800 × 300 comes out front as 2.94 × 10⁶; the varying factor is h(x) = x alone.

questions.q: In the rope example she spends most of the slide constructing F(x) = 0.6468(60 − x) before integrating anything. What makes the '60 − x' the crux of the problem?
options: Only the rope still hanging has to be lifted, so the force needed falls from 38.8 N to 0 as x runs from 0 to 60 — a varying force, which is exactly why the work is an integral
It is the distance the rope still has to travel upwards
It converts the mass per metre into a total mass
It is a change of variable that makes the integral easier to evaluate
questions.concept: Why work by a variable force is an integral
questions.why: The pull only has to support what is still over the edge, and that shrinks as you haul, so F is a function of x rather than a constant, and W = ∫F dx replaces force × distance. Option 2 misreads the variable: x is how much rope has been pulled up, and 60 − x is a length of rope, not a distance yet to be travelled. Option 3 confuses two separate steps — the conversion is 66 g/m to 0.066 kg/m, and it happens before the 60 − x appears. Option 4 treats a piece of physics as a piece of algebra; nothing here is a substitution.

questions.q: In F = ∫ₐᵇ w·h(x)·L(x)dx, what do the three factors stand for?
options: w is the width of the dam, h(x) its height, L(x) its length
w is the weight density ρg of the fluid, h(x) the depth of the strip at position x, L(x) the width of the face at that strip
w is the work done, h(x) the head of water, L(x) the load
w is the mass of the water, h(x) the height above the base, L(x) the perimeter
questions.concept: Reading the three factors of the fluid-force formula
questions.why: w·h(x) is the pressure at depth h(x), and multiplying by the width L(x) and the thickness dx gives the force on one strip; adding the strips is the integral. Option 1 is the trap her own wording invites, since she calls h(x) 'the height of the dam at a point x' while using it as a depth measured down from the surface. Option 3 mixes symbols from different applications. Option 4 gets the direction wrong — measuring height upward from the base would put zero pressure at the bottom, which is the reverse of reality — and w is a density, not a mass.

questions.q: Why can neither CS = ∫₀^Q₀[D(Q) − P₀]dQ nor PS = ∫₀^Q₀[P₀ − S(Q)]dQ be started until the equilibrium has been found?
options: Because the integrals are improper until a finite upper limit is supplied
Because D(Q) and S(Q) are only defined at the equilibrium point
Because both the upper limit Q₀ and the constant P₀ inside the bracket come from solving D(Q) = S(Q)
Because the surpluses are equal at equilibrium, so one determines the other
questions.concept: Equilibrium first, then the surplus integrals
questions.why: Q₀ is the positive root of 1000 − 25Q = 100 + Q², and P₀ = D(Q₀) = 500; without both numbers neither integrand nor either limit is known. Option 1 misuses 'improper', which describes infinite limits or unbounded integrands, not a missing symbol. Option 2 is false — both functions are defined for every Q; equilibrium is just where they agree. Option 4 is false in this very example, where CS = 5000 and PS ≈ 5333 are different numbers.

questions.q: In the copper example she integrates the consumption rate to get C(t) = 1000e^(0.035t) + c, then sets C(0) = 0. What does C(t) count, and what is the condition doing?
options: C(t) is the rate of consumption t years after 2005, and C(0) = 0 says nothing was being consumed in 2005
C(t) is the remaining stock of copper, and C(0) = 0 says the reserves start empty
C(t) is the average annual consumption, and C(0) = 0 fixes the units
C(t) is the cumulative amount consumed since 2005, and C(0) = 0 says nothing has yet been consumed at the moment the clock starts, which forces c = −1000
questions.concept: What the accumulated total counts, and how its initial condition is read
questions.why: The rate is C′(t) = 35e^(0.035t), so its integral C(t) is a running total of copper consumed since 2005; at t = 0 that total is necessarily zero, and since e⁰ = 1 the equation 0 = 1000 + c gives c = −1000, hence C(t) = 1000e^(0.035t) − 1000. Option 1 confuses C with C′ — the rate at t = 0 is 35, not 0. Option 2 reverses the direction: a stock that starts empty could never be exhausted, and part (b) sets C(t) equal to 750, the amount consumed, not what remains. Option 3 misnames an accumulation as an average and gives the condition no real work to do.

questions.q: Name the single idea that all five of this week's applications share, and show it running through three of her examples in three different sets of units.
questions.concept: One idea behind kinematics, fluid force, work, marginal analysis and accumulation
questions.why: A good answer states the idea: if a quantity varies, cut the range into pieces small enough that it is effectively constant on each, multiply on the piece, and integrate to add the pieces — equivalently, the integral of a rate over an interval is the total accumulated over that interval. It should then instantiate it: velocity varies with time, so ∫₀⁵ v dt gives (km/h)(h) = km, the 163.3 km of Example 1; the force on the rope varies with how much has been pulled, so ∫₀⁶⁰ F(x)dx gives (N)(m) = J, the 1164.24 J; marginal revenue varies with quantity, so ∫MR dQ gives (revenue per unit)(units) = revenue, the TR(Q) of the marginal-analysis example. Credit for noticing that the units of the answer are always the units of the integrand multiplied by the units of the variable of integration, which is the fastest check available.

questions.q: Explain why the rope's work cannot be computed as force × distance, and say what number that shortcut would give and why it is wrong.
questions.concept: Why a varying force forbids force × distance
questions.why: A good answer says: force × distance is valid only when the force is the same throughout the motion. Here the pull only has to support the rope still hanging, which is (60 − x) m, so F(x) = 9.8(0.066)(60 − x) = 0.6468(60 − x) newtons — it starts at 0.6468(60) = 38.8 N when the whole rope is over the edge and falls to 0 as the last of it comes up. Multiplying the starting force by the full 60 m gives 38.8 × 60 = 2328.48 J, exactly twice the true answer, because it charges the maximum force for the whole haul. The correct calculation integrates: W = ∫₀⁶⁰ 0.6468(60 − x)dx = 0.6468(3600 − 1800) = 1164.24 J. It is worth adding that the factor of exactly 2 arises because F is linear in x, so the average force is half the maximum — the same reason the dam integral produces x²/2.

questions.q: Her Example 1 calls ∫₀⁵ v(t)dt 'the distance travelled', while Example 2 part (c) calls ∫₀⁵ v(t)dt 'the net displacement'. Explain why both labels are defensible on her own examples, and what a student must be careful about.
questions.concept: Distance versus net displacement, and when they coincide
questions.why: A good answer notices that ∫v dt is a signed quantity — it is always the net displacement — and that it equals the distance only when v does not change sign on the interval. In Example 1, v(t) = 2t² + 6t + 1 is positive for every t in [0, 5], since all three terms are positive, so the car never reverses and the two quantities coincide: 163.3 km is both. In Example 2, v(t) = 6t² − 6t − 12 = 6(t − 2)(t + 1) is negative on (0, 2) and positive on (2, 5), so the two do differ and she correctly says 'net displacement', not 'distance'. The care needed: never assume the two are the same without checking the sign of v, and note that the deck never asks for a total distance and never teaches splitting at the zeros of v, so that technique is background rather than syllabus here.

questions.q: Three of her examples supply an extra piece of data after the integration: x(0) = −4, TR(2) = 260, and C(0) = 0. Say what each is for, and explain what makes the middle one different from the other two.
questions.concept: Initial conditions as equations to be solved for the constant
questions.why: A good answer says all three do the same job — an indefinite integral produces a family of functions differing by a constant, and each datum is an equation that pins the constant down. x(0) = −4: substituting t = 0 into 2t³ − 3t² − 12t + C kills the first three terms, so C = −4 is read straight off. C(0) = 0: substituting t = 0 into 1000e^(0.035t) + c and using e⁰ = 1 gives 0 = 1000 + c, so c = −1000. What makes TR(2) = 260 different is that the condition is not given at zero, so nothing vanishes and it must be solved as a genuine equation: TR(2) = 200 + 40 + 8 + C = 248 + C, and 248 + C = 260 gives C = 12. The examinable warning is that C = 260 is wrong; the given value is the value of the whole function, not the value of the constant.

checks.topic: Conceptual session on Week 12 transformers exactly as the lecturer builds them: the shared core flux and her equation 1, ε₁ = −N₁ dΦ_B/dt and ε₂ = −N₂ dΦ_B/dt; why equal flux per turn gives equal emf per turn and hence equation 2, ε₂/ε₁ = N₂/N₁; the ideal-transformer assumption that upgrades it to equation 3, V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁; step-up as N₂ > N₁ and step-down as N₂ < N₁; the energy statement I₁V₁ = I₂V₂; the squared turns ratio in V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)²; and the hardware facts — iron core, lamination against eddy currents, unchanged frequency, impedance matching for maximum power transfer.

questions.q: Slide 8 writes ε₁ = −N₁ dΦ_B/dt and ε₂ = −N₂ dΦ_B/dt with one and the same dΦ_B/dt. What does the lecturer conclude from that fact?
options: The two windings carry the same current
The primary emf is always the larger of the two
The induced emf per turn is the same in the two coils
The magnetic flux is twice as large in the secondary
questions.concept: Why one shared flux makes the emf per turn equal
questions.why: Dividing each equation by its own N gives ε/N = −dΦ_B/dt, the same number for both coils — her exact words are 'the induced emf per turn is the same in the two coils', and that is what licenses equation 2. Option 1 is contradicted two slides later, where I₁ = 8.0 A and I₂ = 4.0 A in the same example. Option 2 assumes an ordering the equations never fix; which emf is larger depends entirely on which N is larger. Option 4 misreads the shared flux: she says explicitly 'the flux per turn Φ_B is the same in both the primary and secondary'.

questions.q: In the deck's notation, which winding carries the subscript 1?
options: The primary — the side connected to the input AC voltage source
Whichever side has more turns
The side connected to the resistor R
Whichever side is at the higher voltage
questions.concept: Which winding is the primary, independent of voltages and turns
questions.why: Slide 4: 'The side connected to the input AC voltage source is called the primary and has N₁ turns. The other side, called the secondary, is connected to a resistor and has N₂ turns.' Option 2 confuses the label with the turns ratio; in Example 2 the primary has more turns, in Example 1 fewer. Option 3 names the secondary. Option 4 fails on Example 1, where the primary sits at 120 V and the secondary at 240 V. Getting this wrong inverts every ratio in both worked examples.

questions.q: How does the deck define a step-up transformer?
options: One whose secondary current exceeds its primary current
One for which N₂ > N₁
One connected to the higher of the two available supply voltages
One whose core has more laminations than a step-down transformer
questions.concept: Step-up and step-down are defined by turns, not by voltage
questions.why: Slide 9 states it in turns: 'When N₂ > N₁, the transformer is referred to as a step-up transformer. When N₂ < N₁, the transformer is referred to as a step-down transformer.' Equation 3 makes that equivalent to V₂ > V₁, but the definition she gives is the one to quote. Option 1 has it backwards — stepping voltage up steps current down, by I₁V₁ = I₂V₂. Option 3 confuses the supply with the transformer. Option 4 invents a distinction; lamination is about eddy currents and is the same for both.

questions.q: Equation 2 is about emfs: ε₂/ε₁ = N₂/N₁. What does the lecturer add on the next slide before she is entitled to write equation 3, V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁?
options: That the core is laminated so no eddy currents flow
That all voltages are rms rather than peak values
That the frequency is unchanged from primary to secondary
That in an ideal transformer the induced emfs equal the terminal voltages
questions.concept: The ideal-transformer assumption that turns emfs into terminal voltages
questions.why: Slide 9 opens with exactly that sentence: 'In an ideal transformer, the induced emfs ε₁ and ε₂ in the primary and secondary windings are equal to the terminal voltages, respectively.' The move from equation 2 to equation 3 is a physical assumption, not algebra — in a real transformer the terminal voltage differs from the induced emf. Option 1 is a construction detail from slide 5, not the licence for equation 3. Option 2 is a convention about how numbers are quoted; it changes no relationship. Option 3 is true (slide 7) but says nothing about emf versus terminal voltage.

questions.q: According to slide 4, what is the iron core for?
options: To conduct the current from the primary winding into the secondary winding
To increase the magnetic flux and provide a medium for it to pass from one coil to the other
To store the energy that the secondary will later deliver to the load
To hold the two windings apart so that they do not short together
questions.concept: What the core does, and what it does not do
questions.why: Her words: 'The core is used to increase the magnetic flux and to provide a medium for the flux to pass from one coil to the other.' Option 1 describes the commonest misconception about transformers — the windings are never electrically connected; what crosses is flux, not charge. Option 3 turns the transformer into a battery; nothing in the deck stores energy, and slide 10 has power in equal to power out at every instant. Option 4 names an incidental mechanical fact, not the reason iron is used.

questions.q: The core is made of thin sheets of metal insulated from one another. According to slide 5, what does the insulation achieve?
options: It raises the resistance of the secondary winding, reducing heating there
It keeps the primary and secondary circuits electrically isolated
It prevents eddy currents from flowing from one sheet of metal to the next
It increases the flux per turn and so raises the secondary emf
questions.concept: Why the core is laminated
questions.why: Slide 5: the core is laminated 'to minimize eddy current losses ... The insulation prevents the eddy currents from flowing from one sheet of metal to the next.' Eddy currents are the only loss mechanism this deck names. Option 1 confuses the core with the windings; lamination changes nothing about winding resistance. Option 2 is true of a transformer in general and is mentioned on the summary slide, but it is not what lamination is for. Option 4 reverses the effect — lamination is a measure against a loss, not a way of boosting flux.

questions.q: Slide 10 states I₁V₁ = I₂V₂. Read physically, this says that
options: voltage can only be gained at the cost of current, since the power is the same on both sides
the current is the same on both sides whenever the voltages match
the secondary delivers more power than the primary receives, by the turns ratio
the current and the voltage both rise together in a step-up transformer
questions.concept: Power conservation as the reason current moves opposite to voltage
questions.why: The equation says the power input into the primary equals the power output at the secondary, so any factor gained on V must be lost on I. Example 1 shows it: 8.0 A at 120 V and 4.0 A at 240 V are both 960 W. Option 2 states a special case as though it were the content of the equation. Option 3 would make the transformer a source of energy. Option 4 is the single most common exam error — a step-up in voltage is a step-down in current.

questions.q: Slide 11 says a transformer may be used to match resistances between the primary circuit and the load. What is the stated purpose?
options: To make the secondary current equal the primary current
To keep the frequency of the load the same as that of the source
To eliminate eddy current losses in the load
To achieve maximum power transfer between the source and the load resistance
questions.concept: What impedance matching is for
questions.why: Her words: 'This way, maximum power transfer can be achieved between a given power source and the load resistance. In stereo terminology, this technique is called impedance matching.' She then adds that the transformer 'transforms not only voltages and currents, but resistances as well' — the resistance seen from the primary being R/(N₂/N₁)². Option 1 would require a 1 : 1 ratio and has nothing to do with matching. Option 2 happens anyway, at every turns ratio. Option 3 relocates a core loss into the load.

questions.q: Set out the lecturer's three numbered equations in order and say, for each step, what makes the next line follow. Be explicit about where the two minus signs go.
questions.concept: The emf-to-voltage chain, minus signs included
questions.why: A good answer runs: equation 1 is Faraday's law applied to each winding using one shared flux, ε₁ = −N₁ dΦ_B/dt and ε₂ = −N₂ dΦ_B/dt. Dividing the second by the first cancels dΦ_B/dt and cancels the two identical minus signs, giving equation 2, ε₂/ε₁ = N₂/N₁, valid at any instant — the absence of a minus sign there is a cancellation, not an omission. Equation 3, V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁, then follows only after slide 9's assumption that in an ideal transformer each induced emf equals its terminal voltage. It should name equation 3 as the one that carries an assumption, and note that N is a pure count of turns while ε and V are in volts, so both ratios are dimensionless.

questions.q: The deck says transformers 'can only be used with AC'. Justify that from her own equations rather than from memory.
questions.concept: Why a transformer needs a changing flux
questions.why: A good answer points at the derivative in equation 1: the induced emf in each winding is proportional to dΦ_B/dt, not to Φ_B. A steady direct current in the primary sets up a steady flux in the core; a steady flux has dΦ_B/dt = 0, so ε₂ = −N₂ dΦ_B/dt = 0 and nothing is induced in the secondary, no matter how many turns it has or how large the DC is. Slide 7 makes the same point positively — it is the AC source that 'causes a changing magnetic field to be created in the core', and that changing field is what induces the secondary current. The answer should tie this back to slide 3's reason for preferring AC for distribution: only AC voltages can be stepped up for transmission and back down for homes and businesses.

questions.q: Without doing any arithmetic beyond the ratio itself, say which of the lecturer's two examples is step-up and which is step-down, and identify the primary in each. Explain why the appliance's own rating never decides the answer.
questions.concept: Assigning primary and secondary before touching any numbers
questions.why: A good answer says the primary is always the winding connected to the input source. In Example 1 the source is the USA 120-V line, so V₁ = 120 V, and the coffeemaker is the load at V₂ = 240 V, giving N₂/N₁ = 2, which is N₂ > N₁, a step-up transformer. In Example 2 the source is the European 240-V outlet, so V₁ = 240 V, and the dryer is the load at V₂ = 120 V, giving N₂/N₁ = 1/2, which is N₂ < N₁, a step-down transformer. The appliance rating never decides which side is the primary: the coffeemaker is rated 240 V and the dryer 120 V, and each sits on the secondary regardless. It should note that reversing this assignment inverts every ratio, current and resistance in the rest of the example.

questions.q: Explain the formula V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)² in words: what R is, what V₁/I₁ is, and why the turns ratio appears squared rather than to the first power.
questions.concept: Apparent resistance versus load resistance, and why the ratio is squared
questions.why: A good answer identifies R as the load resistance connected across the secondary — the resistor of slide 5, across which V₂ appears — and V₁/I₁ as the equivalent or apparent resistance that the source sees when it looks into the primary, both in ohms. On the square: a resistance is a voltage divided by a current, the turns ratio scales the voltage by N₂/N₁ and scales the current the opposite way by N₁/N₂, so the quotient picks up the factor twice. It should read the consequence off the formula — for a step-up transformer N₂/N₁ is greater than 1, so the load looks smaller from the primary, exactly as Example 1's 60 Ω coffeemaker looks like 15 Ω to the 120 V line — and connect it to slide 11: choosing the turns ratio to make R look like the source's own resistance is impedance matching, done for maximum power transfer.

checks.topic: The Software Testing Life Cycle and Debugging deck: what software testing is and why a defined life cycle is needed at all, the six STLC phases in sequential order with the specific activities each phase owns, entry and exit points, the definition of a test case as inputs, process and expected outputs, and debugging as the process of identifying and resolving bugs together with its named methods (code inspection, monitoring, logging, unit, integration and system testing) and tool categories (debuggers, trace tools, profilers).

questions.q: A tester has finished reviewing the requirement document and the strategy, cost and duration have been signed off. She now writes documents that each list the inputs to supply, the process to follow, and the output that should result. Which phase is she in, and which phase must still be completed before the software can actually be exercised?
options: Test planning; test case development must still be completed
Test environment setup; test execution must still be completed
Test case development; test environment setup must still be completed
Test execution; test cycle closure must still be completed
questions.concept: The order of the six STLC phases and the activities each owns
questions.why: Writing inputs, process and expected outputs is test case development; test environment setup, where the software and hardware are specified, still stands between it and test execution.

questions.q: A team declares the test case development phase closed and moves into test execution, although a third of the written test cases have not yet been reviewed. Which idea from the deck does this most directly violate?
options: The exit point of a phase is reached only when all the objectives of that phase have been achieved, and review of test cases is an objective of test case development
The entry point of test execution is the writing of test cases, so execution cannot begin until every case exists
Test cases may only be reviewed during test cycle closure, so the review is out of sequence
A phase may not be closed until the defects found in it have been corrected, which happens in test execution
questions.concept: Entry and exit points, and the fact that an exit point requires the phase's objectives to have been achieved
questions.why: Identification, writing and review of test cases are the objectives of that phase, so its exit point has not been reached.

questions.q: Which of the following activities belongs to the **test planning** phase rather than to any other phase?
options: Setting up the test data and the hardware on which the tests will run
Assigning roles to the members of the testing team
Interviewing stakeholders about the software requirement document
Collecting feedback and creating the summary report
questions.concept: Which activities belong to which STLC phase
questions.why: Assignment of roles to team members is listed under test planning; a is environment setup, c is requirement analysis, d is test cycle closure.

questions.q: A tester interviewing stakeholders records that the payment provider's sandbox is scheduled to be offline for two of the four planned test weeks. Which phase does this activity belong to, and why does it belong there rather than to test environment setup?
options: Test planning, because anything affecting duration is a planning concern by definition
Test environment setup, because a sandbox is part of the software requirements of the test
Test cycle closure, because an unavailable dependency is a defect that must be reported
Requirement analysis, whose activities include stakeholder interviews and the identification of possible issues that might affect the testing process, before any environment is specified
questions.concept: Requirement analysis: stakeholder interviews and identifying issues that might affect the testing process
questions.why: The deck places stakeholder interviews and identification of possible issues affecting the testing process in requirement analysis, the phase that decides what is to be tested.

questions.q: Both the test execution phase and the test cycle closure phase involve defects and reports. What separates them, as the deck describes their activities?
options: Execution implements the tests, retests to fix defects, and analyses and reports the results; closure checks that the testing objectives have been achieved and the software is ready for use, and produces the summary report and feedback
Execution records defects only; closure is the only phase permitted to correct them
Execution produces the summary report; closure re-runs any test that produced a defect
Execution covers automated tests, closure covers the manual ones, since manual results need human summarising
questions.concept: Test execution versus test cycle closure, and the activities each lists
questions.why: Execution asks whether the tests pass; closure asks whether testing is finished and the software is ready for use, and produces the summary report and feedback.

questions.q: An automated suite reports that `total_due` came back as 4,300 where 4,500 was expected. What has the deck's definition of software testing delivered here, and what remains to be done?
options: Testing has resolved the error; what remains is to confirm that no requirement is missing
Testing has found that the given output differs from the expected output and has located an error; debugging must still identify and resolve the bug that caused it
Testing has identified the bug; debugging will now re-run the suite to confirm the fix
Testing has proved that a requirement is missing, since a wrong total can only come from an unimplemented requirement
questions.concept: Testing versus debugging: detecting a mismatch versus identifying and resolving its cause
questions.why: Testing compares actual with expected output and locates errors; debugging is the separate process of identifying and resolving the bug.

questions.q: A deployed system never crashes and returns correct results, but between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m. its responses become very slow, and no test in the suite fails. Which debugging method from the deck is the natural first move, and on what grounds?
options: Code inspection, because a fault invisible to the tests can only be found by reading the source
Unit testing, because slowness must originate inside a single function's execution paths
Monitoring, because it watches a running system for unusual behaviour or performance issues that indicate the presence of bugs, which is exactly what is observed here
Integration testing, because a symptom that appears only at certain hours must come from the interaction of components
questions.concept: The debugging methods, in particular monitoring for unusual behaviour or performance issues in a running system
questions.why: Monitoring is defined as watching a software system for unusual behaviour or performance issues indicating bugs, which is precisely a load-dependent slowdown no test reproduces.

questions.q: A team can reproduce a fault but cannot see where the program's state first goes wrong, and separately wants to know which routine consumes most of the running time. Which of the deck's debugging tool categories serve these two needs?
options: A profiler for the first, a trace tool for the second
Logging for the first, code inspection for the second
A trace tool for both, since both concern the order of execution
A debugger or trace tool for the first, a profiler for the second
questions.concept: The three debugging tool categories: debuggers, trace tools and profilers, and what each is for
questions.why: Debuggers and trace tools follow execution and state to locate where things go wrong; profilers measure where the time is spent.

questions.q: The deck justifies the STLC by saying that without a standard process which clearly defines the deliverables and objectives of each phase, "we might not be sure that we are testing our software the right way." Explain what specifically goes wrong in a project that tests hard but has no defined phases, and name two phases whose omission would produce the clearest damage.
questions.concept: The rationale for having a software testing life cycle at all
questions.why: Without defined phases nothing states the deliverables and objectives of each stage, so no phase has an exit criterion and the team can never say whether testing is adequate, whether the software meets the set requirements, or whether it is free of defects; effort is spent without a definition of done, and the same ground is retested while other ground is never touched. Omitting requirement analysis is the clearest damage: nobody has decided what is to be tested, so the tests measure the testers' assumptions rather than the requirements. Omitting test case development is next: without written cases specifying inputs, process and expected outputs the results cannot be reproduced, reviewed or handed to anyone else. (Test planning or test cycle closure are also defensible second choices if argued on the same grounds — no roles, cost or duration; or no check that objectives were met and the software is ready for use.)

questions.q: A test case specifies inputs, process and expected outputs. Explain why the *expected output* must be fixed during test case development rather than decided when the test is run, and what would be lost if a tester decided at run time whether the result looked reasonable.
questions.concept: The definition of a test case, and why test case development is a phase of its own
questions.why: Software testing is defined as finding out whether the output the computer gives is the same as the expected output, so the expected output is the standard against which the run is judged; it has to exist before the run or there is nothing to compare against. Fixing it during test case development means it is derived from the requirements and reviewed, which is exactly what that phase's activities — identification, writing and review — are for. If the tester decides at run time whether the result looks reasonable, the actual output silently becomes the expected output: a wrong result that is plausible is accepted, the test is not reproducible by anyone else, and retesting after a fix has no fixed baseline. The judgement also stops tracing back to a requirement, so missing requirements can no longer be detected.

questions.q: Testing and debugging are different processes but the deck lists unit, integration and system testing among the debugging methods. Explain how the same three activities can belong to both, and state what changes about the purpose when they are used for debugging.
questions.concept: Testing versus debugging, and why the same activities appear in both lists
questions.why: The activities are the same mechanically — run part or all of the software on chosen data and compare actual with expected output — but the purpose differs. As testing methods they are used before a bug is known, to find out whether output matches expectation and whether requirements are missing; they are a verification exercise driven by the requirements. As debugging methods they are used after a malfunction is already known, to narrow down where it lives: a unit test isolates a single function so the fault can be attributed to it or ruled out, an integration test decides whether the fault lies in the interaction between components rather than inside either one, and a system test decides whether the whole assembled system still misbehaves. Testing detects and locates that something is wrong; when the same runs are used for debugging they serve identifying and resolving the specific error already observed.

questions.q: Explain the difference between logging and monitoring as debugging techniques, and describe a fault for which logging succeeds where monitoring cannot, and a fault for which monitoring succeeds where logging cannot.
questions.concept: Logging versus monitoring in the deck's list of debugging methods
questions.why: Logging records events and messages related to the software system, so it produces a durable internal record of what the program did and with what values. Monitoring watches the running system for unusual behaviour or performance issues that indicate the presence of bugs, so it observes external symptoms as they happen. Logging succeeds where monitoring cannot on a fault that leaves no outward sign: a rounding error that quietly writes a wrong balance to the database, where the system stays fast and stable but the logged intermediate values show the wrong figure being computed and stored, and the record can be read hours later. Monitoring succeeds where logging cannot on a fault nobody thought to log: memory consumption creeping upward until the process is killed at 3 a.m., or responses degrading only under peak load — no log line was written because the code never anticipated the condition, but the running system's behaviour is visibly abnormal to something watching it.

checks.topic: Computation pass on Week 12: evaluating her seven worked examples and close variants of them — ∫₀⁵(2t² + 6t + 1)dt for the car, x(t) = 2t³ − 3t² − 12t − 4 and the 115 m net displacement, the dam force 2.94 × 10⁶[x²/2]₀¹⁰⁰, the rope work 0.6468[60x − x²/2]₀⁶⁰, TR from MR with TR(2) = 260, the capital growth 4t^(3/2)|₄⁹ that the slide mis-states, and the surplus pair CS = 5000 and PS ≈ 5333 for D(Q) = 1000 − 25Q against S(Q) = 100 + Q².

questions.q: Evaluate ∫₀⁵(2t² + 6t + 1)dt, the distance the car covers in the first 5 hours.
options: 81 km
405 km
330 km
questions.concept: Definite integral of a quadratic velocity
questions.why: The antiderivative is 2t³/3 + 3t² + t, so at t = 5 it is 250/3 + 75 + 5 = 83.33 + 80 = 163.33, and the lower limit contributes 0. Option 2 is v(5) = 50 + 30 + 1 = 81, the speed at the end rather than the distance. Option 3 is that speed times 5 hours, which would only be right if the car held a constant 81 km/h. Option 4 antidifferentiates 2t² as 2t³ instead of 2t³/3, giving 250 + 75 + 5.

questions.q: Using the same car velocity v(t) = 2t² + 6t + 1, how far does it travel in the first 3 hours?
options: 37 km
48 km
84 km
111 km
questions.concept: Applying her method to a new upper limit
questions.why: [2t³/3 + 3t² + t]₀³ = 2(27)/3 + 3(9) + 3 = 18 + 27 + 3 = 48 km, and the lower limit again contributes 0. Option 1 is v(3) = 18 + 18 + 1 = 37, the speed at the end rather than the distance. Option 3 antidifferentiates 2t² as 2t³ without dividing by 3, giving 54 + 27 + 3. Option 4 is v(3) multiplied by 3 hours, which assumes a constant speed the car never has. The habit that protects you is hers: write the full bracket, substitute term by term, then add.

questions.q: A body has v(t) = 6t² − 6t − 12 m/s with initial displacement −4 m. Find x(3).
questions.concept: Substituting into the displacement function, constant included
questions.why: x(t) = 2t³ − 3t² − 12t − 4, so x(3) = 2(27) − 3(9) − 12(3) − 4 = 54 − 27 − 36 − 4 = −13 m. Option 1 is v(3) = 54 − 18 − 12 = 24, substituting into the velocity instead of the displacement. Option 2 forgets the −4, i.e. never used the initial condition. Option 4 solves x(0) = −4 with the wrong sign and uses C = +4.

questions.q: For that same body, evaluate ∫₀⁵(6t² − 6t − 12)dt.
questions.concept: Definite integral of velocity as net displacement
questions.why: [2t³ − 3t² − 12t]₀⁵ = 250 − 75 − 60 − 0 = 115 m. Option 1 is x(5) = 111: the −4 was carried in and subtracted only once, giving the position rather than the change. Option 2 is the total distance — the body goes back 20 m to t = 2 and then forward 135 m — which is not what a signed integral returns. Option 3 is v(5) = 150 − 30 − 12 = 108, the integrand at the upper limit.

questions.q: A 60 m rope of mass 66 g/m hangs over a cliff. Evaluate W = ∫₀⁶⁰ 0.6468(60 − x)dx.
questions.concept: Evaluating the work integral for a linearly decreasing force
questions.why: 0.6468[60x − x²/2]₀⁶⁰ = 0.6468(3600 − 1800) = 0.6468 × 1800 = 1164.24 J. Option 2 is the starting force 0.6468 × 60 = 38.8 N multiplied by the whole 60 m, valid only for a constant force and exactly double the truth because F is linear. Option 3 evaluates the bracket correctly but never multiplies by the coefficient 0.6468. Option 4 adds x²/2 instead of subtracting it, giving 0.6468(3600 + 1800).

questions.q: For the 100 m by 300 m dam with its top at the water surface, evaluate F = ∫₀¹⁰⁰(9800)(x)(300)dx.
questions.concept: Evaluating the fluid-force integral, including the factor of one half
questions.why: Pull the constants out: 9800 × 300 = 2.94 × 10⁶, then [x²/2]₀¹⁰⁰ = 10000/2 = 5000, so F = 2.94 × 10⁶ × 5000 = 1.47 × 10¹⁰ N. Option 1 omits the division by 2 — the same number you get by applying the deepest pressure to the whole face, which overcounts every strip above the base. Option 3 stops at the constant and never integrates. Option 4 uses [x/2] in place of [x²/2] and so loses a factor of 100.

questions.q: MR = 100 + 20Q + 3Q² and TR(2) = 260. Find the constant in TR(Q).
questions.concept: Solving for the constant from a value given away from zero
questions.why: TR(Q) = 100Q + 10Q² + Q³ + C, and TR(2) = 200 + 40 + 8 + C = 248 + C; setting 248 + C = 260 gives C = 12. Option 1 copies the given value straight into C, which is the standard error whenever the condition is given away from Q = 0. Option 2 ignores the condition altogether, which would make TR(2) = 248, not 260. Option 4 loses the Q³ term when substituting, getting 240 + C = 260 — a reminder to check that every term of the antiderivative is evaluated, not just the ones you wrote first.

questions.q: For D(Q) = 1000 − 25Q and S(Q) = 100 + Q², with Q₀ = 20 and P₀ = 500, evaluate the consumer surplus.
questions.concept: Evaluating the consumer-surplus integral
questions.why: CS = ∫₀²⁰(1000 − 25Q − 500)dQ = ∫₀²⁰(500 − 25Q)dQ = [500Q − 25Q²/2]₀²⁰ = 10 000 − 5000 = 5000. Option 1 keeps only the first term, forgetting −25Q²/2. Option 2 is the producer surplus, 16000/3 ≈ 5333 — the two are close in size and easy to swap, so always check which bracket you formed. Option 3 halves the answer, typically by writing 25Q²/2 as 25Q²/4 or by using an upper limit of 10.

questions.q: Evaluate the capital growth K = ∫₄⁹ 6√t dt in full. State what the slide prints as the answer and why that is wrong.
questions.concept: Integrating a square root, and the slide's incorrect final value
questions.why: A good answer rewrites first: 6√t = 6t^(1/2), so n = 1/2, the new power is 3/2, and dividing by 3/2 means multiplying by 2/3 — giving 6 × (2/3) t^(3/2) = 4t^(3/2). Then evaluate: K = 4t^(3/2)|₄⁹ = 4(9^(3/2)) − 4(4^(3/2)). Since 9^(3/2) = (√9)³ = 3³ = 27 and 4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 2³ = 8, K = 4(27) − 4(8) = 108 − 32 = 76. The slide prints the final answer as 4, which is simply the coefficient of t^(3/2) left standing where the number should be; every earlier line of the slide is correct and those lines give 76. Quote 76 and say so plainly, because this misprint will otherwise be copied into an exam script. A student answering 6 has substituted into the integrand, I(9) − I(4) = 18 − 12, instead of into the antiderivative.

questions.q: For D(Q) = 1000 − 25Q and S(Q) = 100 + Q², find the equilibrium quantity and price and then compute the producer surplus, showing the quadratic in full.
questions.concept: Equilibrium by quadratic, then the producer-surplus integral
questions.why: A good answer sets D(Q) = S(Q): 1000 − 25Q = 100 + Q², so Q² + 25Q − 900 = 0. By the formula, Q = (−25 ± √(625 + 3600))/2 = (−25 ± √4225)/2 = (−25 ± 65)/2, giving Q = 20 or Q = −45; a negative quantity is meaningless, so Q₀ = 20. Then P₀ = D(20) = 1000 − 500 = 500, checked against S(20) = 100 + 400 = 500. The producer surplus is PS = ∫₀²⁰[P₀ − S(Q)]dQ = ∫₀²⁰(500 − 100 − Q²)dQ = ∫₀²⁰(400 − Q²)dQ = [400Q − Q³/3]₀²⁰ = 8000 − 8000/3 = 16000/3 = 5333.33, which the slide rounds to 5333. Credit for keeping the bracket the right way round — P₀ minus S(Q) for producers, D(Q) minus P₀ for consumers — and for discarding the negative root explicitly rather than silently.

questions.q: Copper is consumed at the rate 35e^(0.035t) thousand metric tons per year, t years after 2005. Build the cumulative model and find the year in which 750 thousand metric tons have been consumed, showing the logarithm step. Identify the misprint on that slide.
questions.concept: Exponential accumulation model and solving for t with a natural log
questions.why: A good answer integrates the rate: C(t) = ∫35e^(0.035t)dt = (35/0.035)e^(0.035t) + c = 1000e^(0.035t) + c, noting that ∫e^(kt)dt = e^(kt)/k means dividing by k, and 35 ÷ 0.035 = 1000. Applying C(0) = 0 with e⁰ = 1 gives 0 = 1000 + c, so c = −1000 and C(t) = 1000e^(0.035t) − 1000. Then set C(t) = 750: 1000e^(0.035t) = 1750, so e^(0.035t) = 1.750; taking natural logs, 0.035t = ln(1.750) = 0.5596, so t = 0.5596/0.035 = 15.989 ≈ 16 years, and 2005 + 16 = 2021. The misprint is in the slide's last line, which writes the denominator as 0.0035 rather than 0.035; the denominator must be the coefficient in the exponent, because that is what taking logs leaves behind. The printed value 15.989 is right because it was computed with 0.035 — with 0.0035 it would read 159.89 years, i.e. the year 2165, which contradicts the slide's own conclusion.

questions.q: Using her rope set-up unchanged, how much work is done in pulling up only the first 30 m of the 60 m rope? Show the working and say why the answer is more than half of 1164.24 J.
questions.concept: Changing the limits on the work integral, and why the halves are unequal
questions.why: A good answer keeps F(x) = 0.6468(60 − x) and changes only the upper limit: W = ∫₀³⁰ 0.6468(60 − x)dx = 0.6468[60x − x²/2]₀³⁰ = 0.6468(1800 − 450) = 0.6468 × 1350 = 873.18 J. It should then explain the comparison: the force is largest at the start, 38.8 N, and falls linearly to 0.6468(30) = 19.4 N by the halfway point and to 0 at the end, so the first half of the haul is done against the heavier part of the load. Numerically the first 30 m takes 873.18 J and the last 30 m only 1164.24 − 873.18 = 291.06 J, a ratio of exactly 3 to 1 — which is what a linearly decreasing force always gives. The examinable point is that only the limits change; the force function is built once from the physics and then reused.

checks.topic: Problems-only session on Week 12 transformers. Compute with the lecturer's three tools and nothing else: V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁ for turns ratios and voltages, P_av = V₁I₁ together with I₁V₁ = I₂V₂ for currents, and V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)² for resistances. Covers all six part-answers of her two worked examples — 2, 8.0 A, 60 Ω, 1/2, 6.67 A, 36 Ω — the line she leaves out of Example 2(c), fresh numbers on the same three formulas, and one wrong solution to diagnose.

questions.q: Example 1: a 960-W coffeemaker designed for a 240-V line is to run from the USA-standard 120-V line. What turns ratio N₂/N₁ does the lecturer obtain?
questions.concept: Assigning V₁ and V₂ before forming the turns ratio
questions.why: The 120-V line is the source, so V₁ = 120 V, and the coffeemaker is the load, so V₂ = 240 V: N₂/N₁ = V₂/V₁ = 240/120 = 2, twice as many turns on the secondary — a step-up transformer. Option 1 puts the appliance's rating in the primary, which is Example 2's answer, not this one. Option 3 quotes a voltage as if it were a ratio; the turns ratio is dimensionless. Option 4 squares an already inverted ratio, importing the square that belongs only in the resistance formula.

questions.q: Example 1(b): what current does the coffeemaker draw from the 120-V line?
questions.concept: Line current is the primary current, from P_av = V₁I₁
questions.why: P_av = V₁I₁ gives I₁ = P_av/V₁ = 960/120 = 8.0 A. Option 1 is the secondary current, I₂ = 960/240 = 4.0 A — the current in the coffeemaker itself, and the right answer to a question that was not asked. Option 2 halves that again, applying the turns ratio a second time. Option 3 inverts the formula, computing V₁/P_av. Always ask which side of the transformer the question is standing on.

questions.q: Example 1(c): with V₁ = 120 V, I₁ = 8.0 A and N₂/N₁ = 2, what is the resistance of the coffeemaker?
questions.concept: Recovering the load resistance from the apparent resistance
questions.why: V₁/I₁ = 120/8 = 15 Ω, then V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)² rearranges to R = (V₁/I₁)(N₂/N₁)² = 15(2)² = 15 × 4 = 60 Ω. Check: V₂/I₂ = 240/4.0 = 60 Ω. Option 2 stops at the apparent resistance and never applies the formula at all. Option 3 multiplies by the ratio instead of its square, the commonest slip in this calculation. Option 4 divides by the square instead of multiplying, running the formula backwards.

questions.q: Example 2(b): the 1600-W dryer, rated 120 V, is run through a transformer from a 240-V European outlet. What current does it draw from that outlet?
questions.concept: Primary current in the step-down case
questions.why: The outlet is the primary, so I₁ = P_av/V₁ = 1600/240 = 6.67 A (exactly 20/3 A). Option 1 is I₂ = 1600/120 = 13.3 A, the current in the dryer element on the secondary — the mirror of the trap in Example 1(b). Option 2 halves 6.67 A, applying the turns ratio to a current that already accounts for it. Option 3 divides by nothing. Sanity check: I₁V₁ = 6.67 × 240 ≈ 1600 W = I₂V₂ = 13.3 × 120.

questions.q: Slide 21 ends at V₁/I₁ = 240/6.67 = 36 Ω without using the ratio N₂/N₁ = 1/2 it lists. Finish the calculation: what is the dryer's own resistance?
options: 9 Ω
questions.concept: The line the deck leaves out of Example 2(c)
questions.why: R = (V₁/I₁)(N₂/N₁)² = 36 × (1/2)² = 36 × 1/4 = 9 Ω, confirmed independently by R = V₂/I₂ = 120/13.3 = 9 Ω and by V₂²/P_av = 14400/1600 = 9 Ω. Option 1 repeats the apparent resistance, which answers what the dryer appears to have at 240 V, not what it is. Option 2 multiplies by the ratio rather than its square. Option 4 applies the square once more on top of the correct answer. Note that Example 1(c) asked for the appliance's own resistance and Example 2(c) for the apparent one — the deck ends its two examples on different quantities.

questions.q: An ideal transformer has N₁ = 400 turns and N₂ = 100 turns, with 240 V rms applied to the primary. What is the secondary voltage?
questions.concept: Applying V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁ in the direction the question asks
questions.why: V₂ = V₁(N₂/N₁) = 240 × (100/400) = 240 × 1/4 = 60 V, and since N₂ < N₁ this is a step-down transformer, so a secondary voltage below 240 V is what you should expect. Option 1 inverts the ratio, multiplying by 4 instead of dividing — the answer a step-up transformer would give. Option 2 divides by the square of the ratio, 240/16, borrowing the square from the resistance formula where it does not belong. Option 3 divides by 10, a slip in the turns arithmetic.

questions.q: An ideal transformer draws 5.0 A from a 200-V rms supply, and its secondary is at 25 V rms. What is the secondary current?
questions.concept: Using I₁V₁ = I₂V₂ in the correct direction
questions.why: I₁V₁ = 5.0 × 200 = 1000 W, so I₂ = 1000/25 = 40 A: the voltage was stepped down by 8, so the current is stepped up by 8. Option 2 multiplies by 25/200 instead of dividing, treating current like voltage — the single most common error on this equation. Option 3 assumes the current is unchanged, which would violate the power equation. Option 4 quotes the ratio 200/25 itself as though a dimensionless number were an ampere reading.

questions.q: A load of resistance 8.0 Ω is connected across the secondary of an ideal transformer whose turns ratio is N₂/N₁ = 1/4. What resistance does the primary source appear to be driving?
questions.concept: Resistance transformation with a fractional turns ratio
questions.why: V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)² = 8.0/(1/4)² = 8.0/(1/16) = 8.0 × 16 = 128 Ω. Because this is a step-down transformer the load looks larger from the primary, the opposite of Example 1, where a step-up made 60 Ω look like 15 Ω. Option 1 uses the ratio to the first power, 8.0 × 4. Option 2 divides by 4 instead of multiplying. Option 4 divides by 16 rather than multiplying, running the formula in reverse. Dividing by a fraction is what makes this number grow.

questions.q: Work Example 1 in full, all three parts, in the lecturer's own steps, and finish with a check that power is conserved.
questions.concept: The coffeemaker example reproduced end to end
questions.why: A good answer sets V₁ = 120 V (the line, hence the primary) and V₂ = 240 V (the coffeemaker, hence the secondary). (a) N₂/N₁ = V₂/V₁ = 240/120 = 2, so the secondary needs twice as many turns as the primary — a step-up transformer. (b) P_av = V₁I₁ gives I₁ = 960/120 = 8.0 A from the line, and I₂ = P_av/V₂ = 960/240 = 4.0 A in the coffeemaker; the answer to (b) is 8.0 A. (c) V₁/I₁ = 120/8 = 15 Ω, then R = (V₁/I₁)(N₂/N₁)² = 15(2)² = 60 Ω. The check should be explicit: I₁V₁ = 8.0 × 120 = 960 W and I₂V₂ = 4.0 × 240 = 960 W, equal as slide 10 requires, and the current ratio 8.0/4.0 = 2 is the inverse of the voltage ratio. Credit naming which of the three equations each part used.

questions.q: Work Example 2 parts (b) and (c) in full, then add the line slide 21 omits. Say what is exact and what is rounded in the numbers 6.67 A, 13.3 A and 36 Ω.
questions.concept: The hair-dryer example, completed and with its rounding accounted for
questions.why: A good answer sets V₁ = 240 V and V₂ = 120 V. (b) I₁ = P_av/V₁ = 1600/240 = 6.67 A from the outlet, and I₂ = P_av/V₂ = 1600/120 = 13.3 A in the dryer element. (c) V₁/I₁ = 240/6.67 = 36 Ω, the resistance the dryer appears to have at 240 V, which is what the question asked. The omitted line: R = (V₁/I₁)(N₂/N₁)² = 36 × (1/2)² = 9 Ω, the dryer's own resistance, confirmed by V₂/I₂ = 120/13.3 = 9 Ω. On rounding: 1600/240 = 20/3 = 6.666… A and 1600/120 = 40/3 = 13.33… A, so both currents are three-significant-figure roundings; 240 divided by the exact 20/3 is 36 Ω exactly, while 240/6.67 is 35.98, so her 36 Ω is the exact value rather than a rounding of the divided figure.

questions.q: A 25 Ω load is connected across the secondary of an ideal transformer with N₂/N₁ = 5, and 60 V rms is applied to the primary. Using only the deck's formulas, find the resistance seen at the primary, the primary current, the secondary voltage and the secondary current, and verify the power.
questions.concept: Chaining the three deck formulas through one unfamiliar problem
questions.why: A good answer works in the deck's own order. Resistance seen at the primary: V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)² = 25/5² = 25/25 = 1.0 Ω. Primary current: I₁ = V₁ divided by that apparent resistance = 60/1.0 = 60 A. Secondary voltage from equation 3: V₂ = V₁(N₂/N₁) = 60 × 5 = 300 V. Secondary current from slide 10: I₂ = I₁V₁/V₂ = (60 × 60)/300 = 3600/300 = 12 A. Verification: I₁V₁ = 60 × 60 = 3600 W and I₂V₂ = 12 × 300 = 3600 W, equal; and as a second check the load itself takes V₂/R = 300/25 = 12 A, matching I₂. It should note that a step-up of 5 in voltage is a step-down of 5 in current, 60 A to 12 A, and that the 25 Ω load looks like only 1 Ω from the primary because the ratio enters squared.

questions.q: A student answers Example 1(c) like this: 'V₁/I₁ = 120/8 = 15 Ω, and N₂/N₁ = 2, so R = 15 × 2 = 30 Ω.' Diagnose the error, give the correct answer, and describe a check that would have caught it in seconds.
questions.concept: Diagnosing a first-power slip in the resistance formula
questions.why: A good answer identifies the single defective step: the formula is V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)², so rearranging gives R = (V₁/I₁)(N₂/N₁)², and the ratio must be squared — 15 × (2)² = 15 × 4 = 60 Ω, not 15 × 2 = 30 Ω. Everything before that line, including 120/8 = 15 Ω, is correct, so this is one arithmetic move rather than a misunderstanding of the setup. The check: the coffeemaker is a 960-W appliance running at 240 V, so its current is 960/240 = 4.0 A and its resistance is V₂/I₂ = 240/4.0 = 60 Ω, computed without the transformation formula at all; 30 Ω would imply 240/30 = 8 A through the coffeemaker and hence 1920 W, twice its rating. A good answer should say that recomputing the quantity a second way from the secondary side is the general habit worth having here.

checks.topic: Applying the Software Testing Methods deck to real code: classifying a failure as functional or non-functional and choosing the method (unit, integration, system, acceptance versus usability, performance, security, compatibility), choosing the integration direction top-down or bottom-up, deciding between black, white and grey box for a given situation and knowing which levels each applies to, designing test data by equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis, and reading a debugger's breakpoint and variable watch to name the defect class.

questions.q:
A function is specified to accept a whole-number score from 0 to 100 and return a band:

```
def grade(score):
    if score >= 70:  return "A"
    elif score >= 60: return "B"
    elif score >= 50: return "C"
    else:             return "F"
```

Which set of inputs is the one chosen by equivalence partitioning together with boundary value analysis?
options: 0, 25, 50, 75, 100 — five evenly spaced values across the whole permitted range
49, 50, 59, 60, 69, 70, together with 0 and 100 — the value on each side of every band edge, plus the two ends of the input domain
55, 65, 75, 85 — one representative taken from the middle of each band
70, 60 and 50 — the three thresholds alone, since a threshold that behaves correctly guarantees the rest of its band
questions.concept: Equivalence partitioning combined with boundary value analysis when designing test data
questions.why: Partitioning identifies the four bands, and boundary analysis adds the values immediately below and at each edge, plus the ends of the domain — the places where a wrong relational operator shows up; c is partitioning without boundaries, and d is boundaries without the partitions.

questions.q: A registration form is specified to accept applicants aged 18 to 65 **inclusive**. The implementation reads `if age > 18 and age <= 65:`. Which single boundary value exposes the fault, and what class of defect is it?
options: 66, and it is a wrong branch order, because the upper test is evaluated after the lower one
17, and it is an uninitialised-variable defect, because nothing sets a default for under-age input
18, and it is an off-by-one produced by a wrong relational operator, `>` used where `>=` was required
65, and it is an integer-division defect, because the range is compared rather than divided
questions.concept: Boundary value analysis and naming the defect class it exposes
questions.why: Only age 18 distinguishes `>` from `>=`: the spec includes 18 but the code rejects it, an off-by-one at the lower boundary; 17, 65 and 66 all behave identically under both versions.

questions.q: A developer opens the source of `grade` above, counts the four execution paths through it, and picks one input to drive each path. Which method is she using, and which testing levels does the deck say it applies to?
options: White box testing; applicable to unit testing, integration testing and system testing
Black box testing; applicable to integration testing, system testing and acceptance testing
Grey box testing; primarily used in integration testing
White box testing; applicable to acceptance testing only, since every execution path ends in an output the user sees
questions.concept: White box testing: internals known, inputs chosen to exercise paths, and the levels it applies to
questions.why: Choosing inputs to exercise paths through known code is white box, which the deck says applies to unit, integration and system testing — notably not acceptance.

questions.q: A tester reads the source of the `cart` and `pricing` modules to work out which combinations of discount and stock level are interesting, then exercises those combinations only through the application's public checkout page. How should this be classified?
options: Black box testing, because every test was actually run through the exposed interface
White box testing, because the source of both modules was studied before any test ran
Unit testing, because two named modules are the target of the tests

Grey box testing, in which internal data structures and algorithms are used to design the test cases while the testing is done at the user or black-box level, and which is primarily used in integration testing
questions.concept: Grey box testing: internals used to design the cases, execution at the black-box level
questions.why: This is the deck's own grey box example — two modules' code studied to design the cases, the tests then conducted through the exposed interfaces.

questions.q: A team tests the currency-conversion and date helper modules first, then the transaction module that calls them, then the reporting module above that. Which approach is this, and what would the alternative have done?
options: Top-down integration; the alternative would have started with the reporting module
Bottom-up integration, in which lower-level modules are tested first; the top-down alternative would have tested the higher-level modules first
Bottom-up design in the Week 11 sense, which concerns composition of components and says nothing about the order of integration tests
System testing, because all three layers are included by the time the sequence ends
questions.concept: Top-down versus bottom-up integration testing
questions.why: Lower-level modules tested before higher-level ones is bottom-up integration; top-down reverses the order, testing higher-level modules first.

questions.q: A loan page computes interest correctly to the last kobo. With five users it responds in under a second; with five hundred concurrent users it takes forty seconds. Which classification and method does this failure call for?
options: Functional testing has failed, because a forty-second response is not the expected output of the program
Usability testing, because the delay is discovered by observing users while they use the software
Non-functional testing, specifically performance testing, which checks how the software will perform under different load conditions
Compatibility testing, because the software behaves differently in one situation from another
questions.concept: Functional versus non-functional methods, and performance testing under different load conditions
questions.why: The output is correct, so the function is right; what fails is how well it performs under load, which is performance testing — a non-functional method.

questions.q: A tester writes twelve unit tests for a function containing two nested conditionals and a loop. All twelve pass, and she reports the function as proven correct. Assess the claim.
options: Sound, provided the twelve cases were derived from the specification rather than from reading the code
Sound, because unit testing operates on the functions in a program and this is a single function
Unsound, because unit testing is a non-functional method and non-functional methods cannot establish correctness

Unsound, because the deck states that it is practically impossible to test all the execution paths in a software and that the number and type of test data are limited, so passing tests show only that the paths exercised behaved as expected
questions.concept: The stated limitation of unit testing: untestable path coverage and limited test data
questions.why: The deck's limitation is explicit — all execution paths cannot practically be tested and the test data is limited in number and type, so passing tests never amount to proof.

options: `total` ends at 30 rather than 60, because the loop stops one element early; the defect is an off-by-one in the bound given to `range`
`total` ends at 60, and the division then truncates the result; the defect is integer division
`total` is never initialised, so the first addition works on a stale value; the defect is an uninitialised accumulator
`total` ends at 60, and the fault is in `len(scores)`, which yields 3 where 2 is required; the defect is a wrong operator
questions.concept: Reading a debugger's variable watch to locate where state first goes wrong, and naming the defect class
questions.why: `range(len(scores) - 1)` gives i = 0 and 1 only, so total reaches 30 and 30/3 = 10.0; the watch shows 10 then 30 and stops — a classic off-by-one in the loop bound.

questions.q: A payment module has already passed unit tests for every one of its functions, yet the checkout fails as soon as it is wired to the inventory module. Explain why passing unit tests could not have prevented this, name the level of testing that would have caught it, and say which of the two integration directions you would choose here and why.
questions.concept: Unit versus integration testing, and choosing top-down or bottom-up integration
questions.why: Unit testing checks the execution paths within individual functions, mostly on the functions of one module in isolation; it says nothing about how different parts of the software work together, so a mismatch in what the two modules pass to each other — a differently shaped record, a different unit of currency, a different assumption about when stock is decremented — sits entirely outside what any unit test observes. Integration testing is the level that tests how well different parts of a software work together, and is what would have caught it. Either direction is defensible if justified: bottom-up, testing the lower-level payment and inventory modules together first before bringing in the checkout module above them, is the stronger choice here because both modules already exist and are individually tested, so the interface between them is the one unknown and should be exercised directly; top-down would exercise the checkout module first and rely on the lower modules being reached later, which delays the very interaction that is failing.

questions.q: Two testers produce identical sets of inputs for the same login form. One read the source first; the other never saw it. Explain why their tests are not the same kind of test, what each is called, and why the deck says grey box is "primarily used in integration testing".
questions.concept: Black, white and grey box classified by what the tester knows, not by what the run looks like
questions.why: The classification turns on whether the internal structure, design and implementation are known to the tester, not on the inputs that result. The tester who never saw the source is doing black box testing: she works from the outside, supplying inputs and verifying outputs against expected outcomes, and any coverage of the internal paths is incidental. The tester who read the source and used it to pick her inputs is not doing black box testing even though the run looks identical; because she designed the cases from internal knowledge but exercised them through the ordinary interface, she is doing grey box testing — internals partially known, cases designed from data structures and algorithms, testing conducted at the user or black-box level. (Had she also verified the outputs by reasoning about the implementation and driven the paths directly, that would be white box.) Grey box is primarily used in integration testing because that is where its combination pays: the interesting faults live in the interaction between modules, so you need to read both modules' code to know which combinations are worth trying, but you exercise them through the exposed interfaces, which is exactly how the modules meet in the real system.

questions.q: A function is specified to accept a discount percentage from 0 to 50 inclusive. Explain, using this spec, why equivalence partitioning alone would probably miss the most likely defect, which specific values boundary value analysis adds, and what the deck's stated limitation of unit testing implies about how much confidence a passing run of those values earns.
questions.concept: Equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, and the limits of what passing unit tests prove
questions.why: Equivalence partitioning splits the input domain into classes the program should treat identically — below range, valid, above range — and takes one representative from each, say -10, 25 and 80. Those pass under a correct implementation and also under one that wrote `discount < 50` instead of `discount <= 50`, or `> 0` instead of `>= 0`, because 25 is nowhere near an edge; the most likely defect is exactly such an off-by-one at a boundary, and a mid-class representative cannot see it. Boundary value analysis adds the values just below, at and just above each edge: -1, 0, 1 at the lower edge and 49, 50, 51 at the upper. Even with all of these passing, the deck's limitation on unit testing still applies — it is practically impossible to test all the execution paths in a software, and the number and type of test data we can use is limited — so a passing run establishes only that the paths those inputs exercised behaved as expected. It raises confidence at the places defects cluster; it does not prove the function correct, and it says nothing about paths no chosen input reaches.

questions.q: A bank's mobile app returns correct balances, but the branch manager reports that customers on older Android phones cannot complete a transfer, and that new customers abandon the transfer screen halfway. Explain which non-functional method applies to each of the two complaints, why neither is a functional failure, and what a functional failure on the same screen would look like instead.
