questions.concept: Non-functional methods — compatibility and usability — against functional failure
questions.why: The older-Android complaint is for compatibility testing, which determines how compatible the software is with different environments such as different browsers, platforms and operating systems, and ensures it performs as expected across every environment the end users will actually use. The abandonment complaint is for usability testing, which discovers issues with the help of users: users are observed while using the software and the problems they face are identified and addressed. Neither is a functional failure because the program does perform its intended function — on a supported device, driven by someone who gets through the screen, the transfer is computed and the balance returned correctly; functional methods ask whether the program does what is expected of it, while these two ask in what environment it can do it and whether a real person can get it done. A functional failure on the same screen would be the transfer itself being wrong: 5,000 debited from the sender but 500 credited to the recipient, a transfer to a closed account accepted, or the balance not updating after a successful transfer — a case where the actual output differs from the expected output, which unit, integration, system or acceptance testing would catch.

checks.topic: Social vices: crime versus deviance, the theory lists, campus cultism and the kidnapping figures.

questions.q: What separates crime from deviant behaviour in the deck?
options: Crime is violent, deviance is not
Crime violates laws, deviance violates norms and rules
Crime is urban, deviance is rural
They are interchangeable with no difference
questions.concept: Crime breaks social laws; deviance breaks social norms and rules
questions.why: Crime carries legal consequences such as fines or imprisonment; deviance is the broader category of straying from norms. The deck's own mid-lesson question offers the interchangeable option as the wrong answer.

questions.q: Which theory holds that deviance is a consequence of material inequality?
options: Labelling Theory
Structural Functionalism
Social Strain Typology
Conflict Theory
questions.concept: Conflict Theory ties deviance to material inequality
questions.why: Conflict Theory blames material inequality. Labelling Theory blames a deviant label applied to the person, Structural Functionalism calls deviance constructive, and Social Strain Typology works from goals and beliefs about attaining them.

questions.q: Who founded the Pirates Confraternity at the University of Ibadan?
options: Wole Soyinka
Ralph Opara
Olumuyiwa Awe
Pius Oleghe
questions.concept: Soyinka founded the Pirates Confraternity in the early 1950s as a social group
questions.why: Soyinka is named as the founder, with patriotic and philanthropic beliefs, not as a secret cult. Opara, Awe and Oleghe are among the friends listed as co-founders alongside him.

questions.q: What sentence does the deck give for membership of a cult group?
options: 3 years
10 years
21 years
Life imprisonment
questions.concept: Membership or soliciting members carries 21 years; hosting a meeting carries 3
questions.why: Membership of a cult group, or soliciting members for an unlawful society, draws 21 years. The 3-year felony is for allowing a cult meeting in a residence or structure you own.

questions.q: How many kidnapping cases were reported in 2022?
questions.concept: Kidnapping rose from 838 cases in 2018 to 4,600 in 2022
questions.why: Kidnapping quadrupled from 838 in 2018 to 4,600 in 2022. The other two numbers are the armed robbery prison records, which fell from 11,858 in 2013 to 10,249 in 2014.

checks.topic: Future trends applied: Wasm, serverless behaviour, ML types, accessible markup and PWAs.

questions.q:
```html
Send
``` Which WCAG principle does this break?
options: Perceivable, the text cannot be read
Understandable, the label is unclear
Operable, it cannot be reached by keyboard
Robust, it uses an outdated attribute
questions.concept: Operable: every interactive element must work from a keyboard
questions.why: Operable means interactive elements work from various inputs, keyboard included, and a plain div takes no keyboard focus. A real button fixes it; the visible text itself is perfectly perceivable.

questions.q: A page is built entirely from `<div class="nav">` and `<div class="header">`. Which principle suffers?
options: Perceivable, the colours may be too faint
Operable, the links cannot be clicked
Understandable, the wording is complex
Robust, assistive tech cannot tell the parts apart
questions.concept: Robust: semantic HTML for current and future technologies
questions.why: Robust is about working with current and future technologies, and semantic HTML is its named example. The links still click, so this is not an Operable failure; it is structure a screen reader cannot interpret.

questions.q: A serverless function keeps a visit counter in a variable and it keeps resetting. Why?
options: Functions are stateless, so nothing survives a call
A cold start clears it on the first request only
The provider's database rejected each write
Event-driven functions cannot declare variables
questions.concept: Stateless: no server-specific state between invocations
questions.why: Serverless functions keep no server-specific state between invocations, so values held in memory vanish. Blaming cold starts is close but wrong: those explain a slow first call, not data lost every time.

questions.q: The first call after an idle hour takes three seconds; later calls take 100ms. What is this?
options: Vendor lock-in
A cold start
Rate limiting
Automatic scaling
questions.concept: Cold starts as a named serverless challenge
questions.why: A cold start is the delay while the provider spins up a function that has not run recently. Vendor lock-in is the other named challenge, but it is about being tied to one provider, not about latency.

questions.q: A browser photo editor needs near-native speed for filters written in C++. What do you reach for?
options: A jQuery animation plugin
A service worker running the filters
WebAssembly, compiled from the C++
Deep learning in the browser
questions.concept: Wasm for near-native speed from compiled languages
questions.why: Wasm is a binary instruction format compiled from C++, Rust or TypeScript, running at near-native speed. Service workers handle caching, offline access and push notifications, not heavy computation.

questions.q: Does WebAssembly replace JavaScript in the browser?
options: Yes, it compiles JavaScript into a binary
Yes, browsers now run Wasm in place of scripts
No, it only runs outside the browser sandbox
No, it complements JavaScript where speed matters
questions.concept: Wasm complements JavaScript rather than replacing it
questions.why: Wasm exists to fix JavaScript's performance limits for heavy work, and the two run alongside each other. It is not compiled from JavaScript, and it runs inside a sandbox, which is one of its advantages.

questions.q: A support chatbot interprets typed questions and answers them. Which field is that?
options: Computer vision
Natural language processing
Unsupervised learning
Edge AI
questions.concept: NLP handles human language
questions.why: NLP covers computers understanding, interpreting and generating human language, with the chatbot as its example. Computer vision handles images and video, illustrated instead by facial recognition.

questions.q: A bank must show why its model refused a loan. Which trend does that call for?
options: Explainable AI
Edge AI
Quantum machine learning
Deep learning
questions.concept: Explainable AI among the future trends
questions.why: Explainable AI is the trend towards interpretable, transparent and trustworthy models. Edge AI is about running processing near where data is generated for low latency, which says nothing about reasons.

questions.q: Netflix suggesting what to watch next is the example of which application?
options: Personalisation
Fraud detection
Content generation
Search engines
questions.concept: Personalisation among the ML applications
questions.why: Personalisation is the named application, with Netflix recommendations given as its example. Search engines is the neighbouring one, illustrated by Google's RankBrain instead.

questions.q: Closed captions on a course video are named for which group of users?
options: Users with motor impairments
Users with cognitive impairments
Users on slow connections
Users who are deaf or hard of hearing
questions.concept: Accessibility tools and who each serves
questions.why: Captions and subtitles are the accessibility tool named for deaf and hard-of-hearing users. Keyboard navigation is the tool aimed at motor impairments, and plain language at cognitive load.

questions.q: PWAs are built on progressive enhancement. What does that mean in practice?
options: The app installs itself on the first visit
Basic browsers work; capable ones get more features
Features load only after the user signs in
The app is rewritten natively for each platform
questions.concept: Progressive enhancement behind PWAs
questions.why: Progressive enhancement means the app works for everyone, from basic browsers up to advanced devices. Rewriting natively per platform is exactly what a PWA avoids, which is where the cost saving comes from.

questions.q: How does inclusivity go beyond accessibility, in the deck's terms?
options: It targets regulatory compliance such as the ADA
It replaces WCAG with a newer set of rules
It designs for all users, not only disabled ones
It applies to mobile devices rather than desktops
questions.concept: Accessibility versus inclusivity
questions.why: Accessibility makes content usable by people with disabilities; inclusivity designs for all users regardless of ability. Compliance with the ADA is listed as a challenge, not as the definition of inclusivity.

checks.topic: Active listening's three benefits and six techniques, the note-taking tips, and deductive versus inductive reasoning.

questions.q: The Cornell method divides your paper into which three sections?
options: Notes, cues and a summary
Headings, bullets and highlights
Ideas, subtopics and details
Thesis, evidence and conclusion
questions.concept: Cornell splits the page into a cue column, note-taking area and summaries
questions.why: Cornell's three zones are cues, notes and a summary written shortly after the lecture. Main ideas linked to subtopics and details is mind mapping; the last option belongs to the summary card on presentations.

questions.q: Which named benefit of active listening is about grasping a problem's details?
options: Enhanced Understanding
Conflict Resolution
Problem Solving
Continuous Improvement
questions.concept: Problem Solving is the benefit about fully comprehending a problem's details
questions.why: Fully comprehending the details equips the listener to give informed solutions. Enhanced Understanding is about words plus emotions, intentions and context; Conflict Resolution is acknowledging perspectives to find common ground.

questions.q: In the deck's note-taking examples, the arrow symbol stands for what?
options: "with"
"leads to"
"therefore"
"important"
questions.concept: The deck's two abbreviation examples are w/ for with and the arrow for leads to
questions.why: The arrow is given as shorthand for leads to, and w/ for with. The deck warns that such abbreviations are for personal notes and may not be tolerated in formal writings.

questions.q: Which tip creates a visual web linking main ideas to subtopics and details?
options: Highlighting or underlining
Bullet points
Headings and subheadings
Mind mapping
questions.concept: Mind mapping is the visual representation connecting ideas to subtopics
questions.why: Mind mapping builds visual representations linking main ideas to subtopics and supporting details. Highlighting is a colour cue for key terms, bullets make notes scannable, and headings give structure for later retrieval.

questions.q: Deductive reasoning, on the summary card, moves in which direction?
options: General premises to specific conclusions
Specific observations to broad generalizations
Evidence to counterargument
Audience analysis to thesis
questions.concept: Deductive is general to specific; inductive is specific to general
questions.why: Deductive reasoning draws specific conclusions from general premises; the reverse, specific observations to broader generalizations, is inductive. The two named fallacies to watch for are strawman and hasty generalization.

checks.topic: The Young modulus beam experiment: definitions, the depression formula, apparatus and the gradient.

questions.q: Plotting depression Y against mass m, the gradient s gives E how?
options: E = 4 b d cubed s / (g l cubed)
E = g l cubed / (4 b d cubed s)
E = 48 s / (g l cubed)
E = g l cubed s / (4 b d cubed)
questions.concept: E = g l cubed / (4 b d cubed s), with the slope in the denominator
questions.why: Rearranging Y = m g l cubed / (4 E b d cubed) puts E and s both in the denominator, so a stiffer material gives a shallower line. The other options invert or misplace the slope.

questions.q: What is the unit of strain?
options: Pascals
Newtons per metre
Metres per kilogram
It has no unit
questions.concept: Strain is a ratio of lengths and is dimensionless
questions.why: Strain is a relative change in dimension, so it is dimensionless. That is why E, being stress divided by strain, carries the same unit as stress: N/m squared, or pascals.

questions.q: For a rectangular cross-section, the moment of inertia I equals what?
options: b d cubed / 12
d b cubed / 12
b d / 12
b cubed d cubed / 48
questions.concept: I = b d cubed / 12, with the cube on the thickness
questions.why: The cube goes on d, the dimension in the direction of bending, with b the breadth. Substituting this into Y = m g l cubed / (48 E I) turns the 48 into a 4.

questions.q: Which piece of apparatus reads the central depression?
options: The set of masses
The mounts
The dial gauge
The beam
questions.concept: The dial gauge reads the depression Y
questions.why: The four listed items are the dial gauge, beams of different materials, a set of masses and two mounts; only the dial gauge reads Y. The mounts are the supports and the masses supply the load.

questions.q: What is the first mass loaded at the beam's centre?
questions.concept: Loading starts at 50 g and runs to 500 g
questions.why: The procedure starts at 50 g, then 100 g, then 200, 300, 400 and 500 g, giving six points for the best-fit line. 500 g is the last load, not the first.

recapCandidates.topic: An integral of a rate is a SIGNED accumulation, so it returns displacement and never distance; the repair is to split at the zeros of v and add magnitudes, never to take a modulus at the end. And the constant of integration is a physical quantity the rate cannot contain — v(0) in kinematics, the fixed cost C(0) in economics — which is also why the extra cost between two outputs needs no fixed cost at all.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Every early example has a positive integrand, so the signed nature of the integral stays invisible until v changes sign; and the attempted repair, taking the modulus after integrating, cannot recover a cancellation that has already happened inside the integral.
whyQuestions: Why does ∫₃⁷ r(t)dt come out in litres when r is in litres per minute — and what in that unit calculation tells you the answer is an amount rather than a rate?
Why is ∫₀⁴ v dt the displacement rather than the distance, when the same integral over a positive velocity gives both?
Why does |∫₀⁴ v dt| fail to fix it, and what exactly has been lost by the time you reach the modulus?
Why can a(t), known perfectly for every instant, still not tell you v(t) — and what is the physical name of the missing information in the kinematics case and in the marginal-cost case?
Why must the fixed cost be added to get C(5), yet left out entirely to get the extra cost of going from q = 2 to q = 5 — and why is it the same fact about constants that answers both halves?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
States the net change theorem with 'net' doing real work: ∫ₐᵇ r dt = f(b) − f(a) is a balance in which intervals where r < 0 subtract from those where r > 0, which is exactly what displacement means and exactly what distance must not do; confirms the reading dimensionally, (units of r)x(units of t).
Gives the procedure for distance rather than just the formula ∫|v|dt — locate the zeros of v, integrate each sub-interval separately, take the modulus of each result, add — and says why the modulus must go inside: after integrating, the forward and backward motion have already cancelled.
Treats the constant of integration as a physical fact, not notation: antidifferentiation fixes the function only up to +C, so v(0) or C(0) supplies information the rate does not contain; then closes the loop by noting the constant vanishes from every difference, so it matters for a level and is irrelevant to a change.
recapCandidates.workedExample: v(t) = t² − 4t + 3 m/s on [0,4], s(0) = 0. Since v = (t − 1)(t − 3), v > 0 on [0,1), v < 0 on (1,3), v > 0 on (3,4]. Displacement = ∫₀⁴ v dt = [t³/3 − 2t² + 3t]₀⁴ = 4/3 m — nothing further is needed, the integral has already accounted for the backward leg. Total distance: split at t = 1 and t = 3 to get +4/3, −4/3 and +4/3, so the distance is 4 m. The wrong approach, |∫₀⁴ v dt| = 4/3, is the displacement wearing a modulus sign; the split shows the middle leg's −4/3 silently annihilating the first leg's +4/3, and the cheap check is that distance must exceed |displacement| whenever v changes sign. Splitting anywhere else fails: at t = 2 the two pieces are +2/3 and +2/3, giving 4/3 again, because the zeros of v are the only points where cancellation can begin. The same fact in money: with MC(q) = 3q² − 4q + 10 and fixed cost ₦50, C(q) = q³ − 2q² + 10q + 50, so C(5) = ₦175 (a level, fixed cost included) while the extra cost from q = 2 to q = 5 is ∫₂⁵ MC dq = 125 − 20 = ₦105 (a change, fixed cost cancelled). ₦155 pays the rent twice; MC(5) − MC(2) = ₦51 differences the rate instead of accumulating it, the exact analogue of reading v(4) when asked how far the particle went.

recapCandidates.topic: A transformer is not an amplifier. It buys voltage with current at an exactly equal rate, V₁I₁ = V₂I₂, so the turns ratio multiplies voltage by N₂/N₁ and divides current by the same factor — but it transforms a load resistance by the SQUARE of that ratio, (N₁/N₂)²R. And none of it functions on DC, because every volt it produces comes from dΦ/dt.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: The first questions asked about transformers are voltage questions, which the turns ratio answers without ever mentioning current, so the amplifier intuition survives; the power balance then arrives as a second formula to memorise rather than as the reason the first cannot mean what the student thought.
whyQuestions: Why does the transformer equation V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁ hold at all — what is the same for both coils, and what does each turn contribute?
Why must the secondary current go down when the secondary voltage goes up, and what statement of physics fixes the two ratios as exact reciprocals rather than merely opposite in tendency?

Why is a load resistance transformed by the square of the turns ratio when voltage and current are each transformed by only the first power — and can you get the square out of the two rules rather than recalling it?

Why does connecting an 8 Ω loudspeaker directly to an amplifier of 800 Ω internal resistance deliver less power to it than putting a lossy transformer in between, even though the transformer can only waste energy?
Why does a transformer produce nothing at all on DC — and, given that answer, why does the output frequency equal the input frequency no matter what the turns ratio is?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
Derives the turns ratio rather than asserting it: one alternating flux threads every turn of both windings, so each turn carries the same emf −dΦ/dt, giving V₁ = −N₁dΦ/dt and V₂ = −N₂dΦ/dt and hence V₁/N₁ = V₂/N₂; then names the current ratio as a separate statement coming from conservation of energy.
Obtains the resistance rule from the other two in front of the listener: V₁/I₁ = (N₁/N₂)²(V₂/I₂), one factor from the voltage and one from the current, and connects it to impedance matching for maximum power transfer.
Identifies the transformer as a Faraday's-law device throughout, so the AC requirement is a consequence, not an extra rule: steady DC gives dΦ/dt = 0 and zero output; the turns ratio scales the size of the emf but not the rate at which the flux reverses, so the frequency is untouched and a transformer cannot rectify.
recapCandidates.workedExample: A 60 W, 24 V soldering iron run from 240 V rms mains through an ideal transformer with a 1200-turn primary. Turns: N₂ = 1200 x 24/240 = 120 (fewer volts out means fewer turns out; 12 000 inverts the ratio). Currents: in the iron I₂ = 60/24 = 2.5 A, but the mains current comes from the power balance, not the turns ratio — P₁ = P₂ = 60 W so I₁ = 60/240 = 0.25 A. The voltage fell by 10 and the current rose by 10, and 240 x 0.25 = 24 x 2.5 = 60 W on both sides, which is itself the answer to 'does it amplify?'. Resistance: the iron is V₂²/P = 9.6 Ω, but the mains sees V₁/I₁ = 240/0.25 = 960 Ω = 10² x 9.6 — the square appears because the source supplies 10x the voltage AND 1/10 the current, and 10 divided by 1/10 is 100; 96 Ω uses the first power. Same physics at scale: 100 kW down a 4.0 Ω line at 1.0 kV means I = 100 A and I²R = 40 kW wasted; at 10 kV, I = 10 A and the waste is 400 W — a hundredfold saving for a tenfold voltage, because V enters twice, once in I = P/V and again because the heating is quadratic. The delivered 100 kW is identical in both cases: the transformer bought nothing, it just moved the power as a small current at high voltage.
